discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 accuracy

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

motivation: Katori proposed the optical lattice clock and its 'magic wavelength': neutral atoms are trapped so strongly that motional effects vanish, while the clock transition is left unperturbed. He demonstrated it with strontium. Ye turned the idea into the world's most precise timekeepers. His work included degenerate Fermi-gas clocks, systematic uncertainties below 10^-18 and the resolution of gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample. Together they brought the laser cooling and trapping of atoms to its most demanding application. Their clocks improve on caesium standards by more than two orders of magnitude and are driving the redefinition of the SI second. They are also used for relativistic geodesy, searches for dark matter, and tests of whether fundamental constants vary. They also opened many-body physics in clock systems. As someone who helped build Latin America's first atomic clock, I regard this as a transformative experimental achievement.
